waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Lake / Yellow Aster Butte Trailhead
waypoints.note: On FR 3065 (Twin Lakes Road), 4.5 mi up from SR 542, where the road continues about 2 rough miles to Twin Lakes; Northwest Forest Pass required and roadside parking along the switchbacks is very limited.
waypoints.directions: From Glacier, follow SR 542 (Mount Baker Highway) east about 12 miles and turn left onto Twin Lakes Road (FR 3065) at the east end of the WSDOT Shuksan maintenance facility. Drive 4.5 miles up the switchbacks to the Tomyhoi Lake / Yellow Aster Butte Trailhead, where roadside parking is limited. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Signed fork below Gold Run Pass: right climbs over the pass and drops to Tomyhoi Lake, route stays left toward Yellow Aster Butte meadows.
waypoints.directions: Start on the Yellow Aster Butte trail and climb steeply — roughly 1,500 ft in the first mile and a half — through an avalanche path and then forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal creeks low down that are the easiest water on the route early in the season. At the signed fork the right branch carries on over the pass and down to Tomyhoi Lake; stay left for the Yellow Aster meadows.

waypoints.name: Yellow Aster tarns / meadows
waypoints.note: High plateau of small glacier-carved tarns; all camping must be at or beyond this point (LNT-only, camp on snow/rock/bare ground, not the fragile meadow turf) — reliable water from the tarns.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the fork the grade eases and the trail traverses the south flank of the butte for a bit over two miles as the terrain opens into meadow. At an unsigned junction around three and a half miles the path to the butte's summit goes right; drop left instead on narrow, steep switchbacks into the tarn basin.

waypoints.name: Boot path onto Tomyhoi Arm
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here and pick up the well-defined climbers' boot path heading north along the crest of Tomyhoi Arm toward the southeast ridge.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the basin and head north-northwest, over a broad hump and down to a col near 6,270 ft, where a well-beaten climbers' boot path picks up along the crest. Getting onto the right crest is the thing to be careful about here — the arm runs north toward the peak, and the trail system does not go that way.

waypoints.name: Moat below Tomyhoi Glacier remnant
waypoints.note: Shallow moat/hard snow between rock and the shrinking glacier remnant — usually the crux; carry an ice axe, and it can be bypassed 100-200 ft lower via a rock finger if snow is firm.
waypoints.directions: Follow the boot path up the broadening ridge, and where the crest narrows above roughly 6,800 ft drop onto the broad benches on the north side rather than staying on top. The path fades into scree and talus as you near the toe of the glacier remnant; traverse along its upper edge to get past several rock pinnacles, assessing the ice before committing to it. Cross the moat between rock and ice — it is hard snow more often than not, which is why an axe belongs on this route, and if it is too firm it can be turned a hundred feet or two lower on a finger of rock.

waypoints.name: Notch below the false summit
waypoints.note: Gain this notch via a V-shaped Class 3.5 slot (some parties belay it), then traverse a ledge west to a wide corner leading up to the false summit.
waypoints.directions: Above the moat, gain the notch through a V-shaped slot of about Class 3.5. It is short but steep and exposed enough that parties often put a rope on it, and it is distinctly harder to reverse than to climb. From the notch, traverse a ledge west to the wide corner that leads up to the false summit.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Peak
waypoints.note: Class 3 scramble on solid rock from the false summit to the true summit block; sweeping views of Mt. Baker, Mt. Shuksan, and north into Canada.
waypoints.directions: From the false summit the true summit looks worse than it is. Downclimb loose ledges to the col between the two, then scramble the summit block on solid, glacier-polished rock — Class 3, with a short gabled section of ridge where the exposure is real on both sides. This is out-and-back ground, so everything climbed here has to be reversed on tired legs.
